# Species richness

## What is species richness?

Species richness $SR_i$ at site $i$ is the number of species recorded:

\begin{equation}
SR_i = \sum_{j=1}^{m} y_{ij} \quad \text{(for binary data)}
\end{equation}

\pause

It is by far the most common biodiversity metric: simple to calculate, intuitive to interpret, and widely used in conservation and ecology.

\pause

But it is a \textbf{derived quantity} from multivariate community data. Analyzing it directly means throwing away most of the data.

## The typical approach

Species richness is most commonly analyzed with Poisson or negative-binomial regression:

\begin{equation}
\log(\mathbb{E}(SR_i)) = \alpha + \textbf{x}_i^\top \symbf{\beta}
\end{equation}

\pause

This is simple and interpretable. But it rests on four assumptions that are routinely violated in practice:

1. Species are \textbf{independent} of each other
2. All species respond \textbf{identically} to the environment
3. The species pool is \textbf{infinite} (unbounded distribution)
4. The Poisson or NB distribution is \textbf{appropriate}

## Assumption 1: species independence

Species are not independent; they share environmental responses and co-occur non-randomly. \newline

\pause

If species co-occurrence is positive, species richness has \textbf{less} variance than a Poisson.
If it is negative, species richness has \textbf{more} variance.

\pause

A Poisson or NB regression cannot accommodate this: it will over- or underestimate uncertainty.

## Assumption 2: homogeneity of niches

A Poisson or NB distribution for species richness is only justified if all species respond the same way to the environment, i.e., have the same niche.

\pause

This is ecologically unrealistic: species have different distributions, different ranges, different optimums.

\pause

The consequence: estimated coefficients from a Poisson richness regression are a \textbf{weighted average} over species, with weights depending on the distribution of species' niches, usually not the average ecologists want.

## Assumption 3: an infinite species pool

A Poisson distribution is unbounded above: it can predict species richness larger than the number of species in your data.

\pause

\textbf{This is ecologically impossible.} You cannot observe more species than those you have observed. \newline

Negative-binomial adds overdispersion, making the problem worse. \newline

\pause

Species richness is inherently bounded by the number of species in the observed pool.

## The correct distribution: Poisson-Binomial

Under species independence and Bernoulli responses, species richness follows a \textbf{Poisson-Binomial distribution}:

\begin{equation}
SR_i \sim \mathcal{PB}(\pi_{i1}, \pi_{i2}, \ldots, \pi_{im})
\end{equation}

with

\begin{equation}
\mathbb{E}(SR_i) = \sum_{j=1}^{m} \pi_{ij}, \qquad \text{var}(SR_i) = \sum_{j=1}^{m} \pi_{ij}(1-\pi_{ij})
\end{equation}

\pause

- Mean species richness = \textbf{sum of species' occurrence probabilities}
- Variance is bounded (cannot exceed $m/4$)
- This is the distribution that actually generates species richness data
- The Binomial is a special case (all $\pi_{ij}$ equal)

## Why univariate analysis fails

\columnsbegin
\column{0.5\textwidth}

```{r pb_vs_pois, echo=FALSE, fig.height=5, message=FALSE}
set.seed(42)
m <- 30
pi_j <- rbeta(m, 2, 5)
pb_mean <- sum(pi_j)
pb_var <- sum(pi_j*(1-pi_j))

k <- 0:m
# Poisson-Binomial via simulation
pb_sim <- replicate(10000, sum(rbinom(m, 1, pi_j)))
pois_pmf <- dpois(k, pb_mean)

par(mar=c(4,4,2,1))
hist(pb_sim, breaks=seq(-0.5, m+0.5, 1), freq=FALSE,
     col="steelblue", border="white",
     xlab="Species richness", ylab="Probability",
     main="Poisson-Binomial vs. Poisson")
lines(k, pois_pmf, col="firebrick", lwd=2, type="b", pch=16)
legend("topright", legend=c("True (Poisson-Binomial)","Poisson approximation"),
       fill=c("steelblue", NA), lty=c(NA,1), col=c(NA,"firebrick"),
       pch=c(NA,16), border=c("steelblue",NA), bty="n")
```

\column{0.5\textwidth}

\footnotesize

The Poisson distribution:

- Puts probability mass on impossible values (SR > m)
- Has the wrong shape (underdispersed here)
- Assumes the wrong mean-variance relationship

The mismatch worsens when species niches are heterogeneous.

\columnsend

# Multispecies modeling

## Species richness as an emergent property

With a multispecies model, we do not model species richness directly. \newline

Instead, we model each species' response to the environment, and \textbf{species richness emerges}:

\begin{equation}
\mathbb{E}(SR_i) = \sum_{j=1}^{m} \mathbb{E}\{I(y_{ij} > 0)\} = \sum_{j=1}^{m} p(y_{ij} > 0)
\end{equation}

\pause

- No separate richness model needed
- Works for any data type: binary, counts, cover, biomass, ordinal
- Uncertainty propagates naturally from species-level predictions
- Assumptions are explicit and testable

## Works for any data type

For any distribution with zero support, the probability of presence can be derived:

| Data type | Distribution | $p(y_{ij} > 0)$ |
|---|---|---|
| Binary | Bernoulli | $\pi_{ij}$ |
| Count | Poisson | $1 - e^{-\mu_{ij}}$ |
| Count | Negative-binomial | $1 - (1 + \mu_{ij}/k)^{-k}$ |
| Biomass | Tweedie | $1 - \text{Tw}(0; \mu_{ij}, \phi_j, p)$ |
| Cover | Ordered beta | $1 - \rho_{ij}^0$ |

\pause

The only requirement: the distribution must assign probability mass at zero (i.e., encode absences).

## Implementation in gllvm

The `predictSR()` function computes:

- Expected species richness $\hat{S}_i = \sum_j \hat{p}_{ij}$
- Full Poisson-Binomial distribution at each site
- Prediction intervals from the distribution
- Optionally for new predictor values

```{r, eval=FALSE}
sr_pred <- predictSR(model, newX = newdata)
sr_pred$expected     # expected species richness
sr_pred$lower        # lower prediction bound
sr_pred$upper        # upper prediction bound

plot(sr_pred)        # predicted vs observed
residuals(sr_pred)   # Dunn-Smyth residuals
```

## Rare species

Species with very low occurrence probability $\pi_{ij} \ll 1$ contribute negligibly to:

- Expected species richness ($\pi_{ij}$ is small)
- Variance of species richness ($\pi_{ij}(1-\pi_{ij}) \approx \pi_{ij}$)

\pause

This means community data can often be trimmed of the rarest species without much effect on richness predictions, but with care: rare species may define range limits and gradient lengths.

\pause

\textcolor{red}{This does not mean rare species are unimportant ecologically: only their contribution to predicted richness is small.}

# Diversity components

## Alpha, beta, gamma diversity

The variance parameters from multispecies models connect to ecological diversity concepts:

\vspace*{\baselineskip}

**Alpha diversity**: average within-site variation, determined by $\sigma^2_\alpha$ (intercept variance) and environmental gradients

**Beta diversity**: between-site variation (how much sites differ in composition); driven by $\sigma^2_\beta$ (slope variance)

**Gamma diversity**: total variation across all sites, the sum of alpha and beta contributions

\vspace*{\baselineskip}

\pause

An effect with higher variance has a larger impact on community composition.

## Connecting model parameters to diversity

For a simple model $\eta_{ij} = \alpha_j + x_i\beta_j$ with $\alpha_j \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2_\alpha)$ and $\beta_j \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2_\beta)$:

\vspace*{\baselineskip}

**Alpha**: $\text{var}(\eta_{ij}) = \sigma^2_\alpha + x_i^2\sigma^2_\beta$

\vspace*{\baselineskip}

**Beta** (turnover between sites $i$ and $k$): $\text{cov}(\eta_{ij}, \eta_{kj}) = \sigma^2_\alpha + x_i x_k \sigma^2_\beta$

\vspace*{\baselineskip}

**Gamma**: $\text{var}_{ij}(\eta_{ij}) = \sigma^2_\alpha + \sigma^2_\beta\{\bar{x}^2 + \text{var}(x_i)\}$

\pause

The variance components directly measure the ecological importance of effects on diversity.

## Variation explained by the ordination

For a JSDM or ordination, the residual covariance matrix captures unexplained species associations:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
getResidualCov(model)$trace   # total residual variation
```

This is the analog of "variation explained" in classical ordination. \newline

\pause

We can also use $R^2_{GLMM}$ and repeatability \footnotesize (Nakagawa and Schielzeth 2013) \normalsize to partition variance across model components.

# Example

## Example: alpine plants in Switzerland

```{r alpine_dat, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE}
Y <- read.csv("../data/alpineY.csv")[,-1]
X <- read.csv("../data/alpineX.csv")[,-1]
X <- X[rowSums(Y) > 0, ]
Y <- Y[rowSums(Y) > 0, ]
X_scaled <- data.frame(scale(X[, sapply(X, is.numeric)]))
```

- Data by [D'Amen et al. (2018)](https://nsojournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/epdf/10.1111/ecog.03148)
- Occurrence of 175 species at 840 plots
- Binary data (presence-absence)
- Sampled on an elevation gradient in Switzerland

```{r}
dim(Y)
```

## Example: fit a JSDM

\footnotesize

```{r jsdm_fit, cache=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
model <- gllvm(y = Y, X = X_scaled,
               formula = ~ELEV,
               num.lv = 2,
               family = "binomial",
               sd.errors = FALSE,
               optim.method = "L-BFGS-B")
```

We include elevation as a covariate and two latent variables to capture residual species associations.

## Example: predict species richness

\footnotesize

```{r sr_pred, cache=TRUE}
elev_seq <- seq(min(X_scaled$ELEV), max(X_scaled$ELEV), length.out = 100)
newX <- data.frame(ELEV = elev_seq)

sr <- predictSR(model, newX = newX)
```

```{r sr_plot, echo=FALSE, fig.height=4, message=FALSE}
obs_sr <- rowSums(Y)
par(mar=c(4,4,1,1))
plot(X_scaled$ELEV, obs_sr, pch=16, col=rgb(0,0,0,0.3),
     xlab="Elevation (scaled)", ylab="Species richness",
     main=NA)
lines(elev_seq, sr$expected$fit, col="firebrick", lwd=2)
lines(elev_seq, sr$expected$lower, col="firebrick", lwd=1, lty=2)
lines(elev_seq, sr$expected$upper, col="firebrick", lwd=1, lty=2)
legend("topright", legend=c("Observed", "Predicted (± 95%)"),
       pch=c(16,NA), lty=c(NA,1), col=c(rgb(0,0,0,0.3),"firebrick"), bty="n")
```

## Example: residual diagnostics

\footnotesize

```{r sr_resid, fig.height=4, message=FALSE}
plot(residuals(sr))
```

Quantile residuals from the Poisson-Binomial distribution: if the model is well-calibrated for species richness, these should follow a standard normal distribution.

## Predicting diversity

As we have explicit equations for diversity, we can predict it using the model.

We take the parameter estimates for the variances, plug-in new values for the covariates (account for scaling), and put it on a map.

\footnotesize

```{r maprep, echo = FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
avi_dat <- read.csv('../data/SwissBirds.csv')
y_birds <- as.matrix(avi_dat[,1:56])
X_birds <- avi_dat[,-c(1:56)]
X_birds <- X_birds[rowSums(y_birds)>0, ]
y_birds <- y_birds[rowSums(y_birds)>0,]
X_birds <- X_birds[,-which(apply(X_birds,2,anyNA))]
X_birds <- data.frame(sapply(X_birds,function(x)if(is.numeric(x)){scale(x)}else{x}, simplify = FALSE))
model_birds <- gllvm(y_birds, X = X_birds, formula = ~(slp+asp|1),
                     family = "binomial", num.lv = 0, beta0com = TRUE)
slp_scale <- scale(avi_dat$slp)
asp_scale <- scale(avi_dat$asp)
source("../1Tuesday/switzerland/slope.R")
x = as.matrix(data.frame(1,(values(slope)-attr(slp_scale,"scaled:center"))/attr(slp_scale,"scaled:scale"),(values(aspect)-attr(asp_scale,"scaled:center"))/attr(asp_scale,"scaled:scale")))
alpha = slope
terra::values(alpha) = rowSums(x*(x%*%model_birds$params$sigmaB))
```

## Predicting alpha diversity

```{r map, dpi = 300, echo = FALSE, cache = TRUE, warning=FALSE,message=FALSE}
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)
library(dplyr)
dat <- as.data.frame(alpha,xy=TRUE) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = -c(x, y), names_to = "layer", values_to = "value")

plt<-ggplot() +
  theme_classic()+theme(axis.text=element_blank(), axis.ticks=element_blank())+scale_fill_viridis_c(name="Alpha diversity", na.value="white")+geom_raster(data=dat, aes(x=x, y=y, fill = value), interpolate=TRUE)+coord_fixed()+xlab(NULL)+ylab(NULL)+ggtitle("Bird alpha diversity (due to mean abundance, aspect and slope)")
plt
```

# Summary

## Summary

- Univariate species richness analyses make strong and routinely violated assumptions
- The correct distribution for species richness is the Poisson-Binomial
- Multispecies models provide a principled framework: richness emerges from species-level predictions
- Works for any data type; uncertainty propagates naturally
- Variance components connect to alpha, beta, and gamma diversity
- `predictSR()` in gllvm implements this framework

\pause

\centering

\textbf{Modelling species richness well requires modelling species well first.}
